name: Street Custom 'Molotov Standard' Incendiary Bottle
description: The oldest improvised weapon still in active use — a glass bottle filled with flammable liquid with a cloth wick. In 2200, the Molotov has evolved: Tier 1 chemists mix industrial solvents with gelling agents to create sticky napalm variants that burn hotter, longer, and cling to surfaces. The weapon remains effective against vehicles, barricades, and personnel because fire does not care about armor ratings or augmentation levels. It is the great equalizer of asymmetric conflict.
specifications:
fuel: Gelled industrial solvent mix
burn temperature: 800-1200°C depending on formulation
burn duration: 30-90 seconds
splash radius: 2-3 meters
weight: 0.5-1 kg
cost: Φ2-10 in materials
construction time: 5 minutes
story_hooks: A coordinated Molotov attack using a new adhesive gel formulation has set an entire corporate checkpoint ablaze — the gel cannot be extinguished with water and sticks to riot shields.
A chemist in Tier 1 has developed a Molotov formula that burns with a specific color based on chemical additives — gangs are using color-coded fire as territorial signals visible across districts.

physical_description.visual_profile: A simple glass bottle silhouette with an asymmetrical, hand-wrapped cloth wick protruding from the neck — deceptively crude yet purposeful. The amber or clear glass catches light, revealing the viscous amber-to-dark fluid sloshing inside. No refinement, pure street pragmatism.
physical_description.dimensions: Height: 18-24 cm, Diameter: 8-10 cm (bottle body), Wick extends 3-5 cm above rim
physical_description.weight_description: Substantial but not unwieldy — 0.5-1 kg of dense, sloshing liquid gives it a satisfying heft without fatigue. Balanced low, stable when held.
physical_description.primary_material: Salvaged or mass-produced glass bottle (common liquor or industrial containers), cotton or synthetic cloth wick, polymeric thread or wire wrapping at neck
physical_description.finish: Raw, unrefined — glass shows fingerprints and dust. Cloth wick is slightly singed at edges from testing or handling. Minimal protection on bottle body; some examples show threadbare wrapping at stress points.
physical_description.color_scheme: Amber or clear glass revealing deep amber, dark orange, or rust-red gelled fuel inside. Wick is off-white, cream, or charred gray. Wrapping around neck in dull blacks, grays, or industrial tape colors.
physical_description.grip_texture: Bare or wrapped glass — smooth, cool, slightly oily from fuel residue. Cloth wrapping at neck provides minimal grip texture, rough hemp or synthetic binding.
distinctive_features: Visible fuel meniscus sloshing behind glass
Hand-wrapped cloth wick with frayed edges
Dark staining around bottle mouth from repeated wick soaking
Occasional chemical-burn marks on glass exterior
Simple knot or twist-tie securing wick to bottle rim
Wear marks from repeated handling and transport in pockets or satchels
Translucent polymer tape or electrical wrap reinforcing weak points
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: None intentional — some bottles retain original manufacturer logos (beer, industrial solvent brands) beneath the fuel staining. Street chemists sometimes scratch initials or small symbols into glass for personal marking.
physical_description.condition_typical: Deliberately rough — scuffed glass, singed wick, minor leakage stains at cap or neck. Appears hastily assembled, ready for immediate deployment. No attempt at cosmetic finish; pure functionality.
